why: Eight black tiles and seven white tiles give 8(-2)+7(2)=-2, agreeing with B; Signed Integers Inside Expressions and Example 1 teach the signed arithmetic.
Repeated multiplication gives 100,000+10,000,000=10,100,000, agreeing with D; Prime Powers and the worked factorization example explain how to expand powers before adding.
The prices are 15/0.20=75 and 75/0.30=250, so their difference is 175, agreeing with B; the percentage-base example teaches reverse division and Discounted Prices identifies the discount base.

type: Shares of totals and a new ratio
why: Green is 50/10=5 and yellow is 120(5/12)=50, giving 10:1 and agreeing with D; Example 1 teaches finding shares by adding, dividing, and multiplying ratio parts.

The units digits repeat 2,4,8,6 and 27 leaves remainder 3 on division by 4, giving 8 and agreeing with E; the only worked power-cycle example uses complex numbers and no lesson applies cycles to ordinary units digits.
Since 72=2^3 times 3^2, its distinct prime divisors are 2 and 3, agreeing with C; the factorization example explicitly groups repeated primes by base.
The 5 by 5 grid contains 25+16+9+4+1=55 squares, agreeing with E; no active lesson works through counting positions separately for each square size.

The square area is 8^2=64 and 4^3=64 gives a cube edge of 4 cm, agreeing with D; Measurement gives forward volume examples but no inverse cube-edge example, while the worked cube root appears inside negative fractional powers.

The circle has radius 2 and area 4 pi while four corner triangles leave a midpoint square of area 16-4(2 times 2/2)=8, giving 4 pi-8 and agreeing with A; Examples 2, 4, and 5 teach triangle area, nested-region subtraction, and adding pieces.

LCM(15,20)=60 minutes gives shared airings at 9 AM through 5 PM inclusive, totaling nine and agreeing with C; the shuttle example teaches shared schedules and the term-count example includes both endpoints.
Doubling length, width, and height multiplies volume by 2 times 2 times 2=8, agreeing with E; Combined Regions and Scaling and Example 11 explain and work through cubic scaling.

type: Whole rectangular pieces from a sheet
why: The area bound is floor(60/8)=7 and seven 4-by-2 pieces fit along the 15-inch length with 1 inch left over, agreeing with B; rectangle-area examples do not teach whole-piece bounds or checking that a cutting layout attains them.

type: Floor tiles with mixed length units
why: A 50-cm tile has side 0.5 m, so 80/0.25=320 tiles are needed, agreeing with B; Example 5 teaches mixed-unit areas but no worked example divides a floor into tiles or checks row and column counts.

Thirty minutes is half an hour, so the separation is (120-80)(0.5)=20 km, agreeing with B; the chase example works through the speed difference and both lessons explain matching time units and using final separation.

The minute hand makes 12 turns in 12 hours, each of length 2 pi(5), giving 120 pi cm and agreeing with B; Example 1 teaches circumference but no worked example connects a clock hand to turns and total travel.

From 6:51 AM to 12:51 PM is six hours and then to 2:27 PM is 1 hour 36 minutes, giving 7 hours 36 minutes and agreeing with C; no active lesson teaches elapsed clock time across noon or borrowing 60 minutes.
Removing two 1-inch margins from each dimension leaves 6.5 by 9 inches and area 58.5 square inches, agreeing with A; the area examples do not work through reducing both dimensions for margins.
Eight points give 8 times 7 divided by 2=28 segments, agreeing with D; Combinatorics Example 7 explains unordered pairs and division by two with a worked two-person committee count.

The tenth figure is 12 by 12 and has 12^2-10^2=44 border tiles, agreeing with C; number-pattern and arithmetic-term examples teach numerical extension but do not demonstrate extracting a border count from a growing diagram.

type: Compare polygon areas on a dot grid
why: Measurement Examples 2 and 5 teach triangle area and decomposition but no worked dot-grid comparison; the official key is C, which cannot be independently checked because the transcript omits the diagram and source-page retrieval failed.

Using 2,4,5,6,9 once in a three-digit minus two-digit subtraction gives the minimum 245-96=149, agreeing with official C at https://cmc.pshs.edu.ph/images/docs/NCE-Sample_Test_Questions-2015.pdf; the digit lesson teaches place value but its worked reversal example does not teach optimizing digit placement.

Using the given offset, 21:20 minus 7:30 is 13:50 or 1:50 PM, agreeing with official B at https://cmc.pshs.edu.ph/images/docs/NCE-Sample_Test_Questions-2015.pdf; no active lesson teaches ahead-or-behind clock offsets or hours-and-minutes subtraction.
